prompt.text:
Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-11.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
The field of 4D portrait avatar reconstruction is currently bifurcated by a trade-off between accessibility and fidelity. On one end, photogrammetry and neural rendering techniques produce high-fidelity, physically consistent results but require elaborate, synchronized multi-camera arrays that are inaccessible to most users. On the other end, generative single-image methods are highly accessible but often suffer from "hallucination" artifacts, lack of temporal consistency, and poor geometry when the head rotates to occluded angles (such as the back of the head). There is currently no unified framework that scales seamlessly—allowing users to utilize anywhere from a single snapshot to hundreds of reference images—to produce a photorealistic, animatable avatar that renders in real-time.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose to bridge the gap between sparse-input generation and dense-input reconstruction by decoupling the two phases. Our core hypothesis is that a **Morphable Multi-View Diffusion Model (MMDM)** can serve as a "universal bridge." By conditioning a diffusion model on robust 3D Morphable Model (3DMM) priors, we believe we can synthesize a dense, highly consistent multi-view dataset from sparse inputs. We hypothesize that if we can generate hundreds of consistent synthetic views covering various poses and expressions, we can then treat this synthetic data as "ground truth" to train a real-time, high-fidelity 4D avatar using explicit 3D representations, thereby combining the semantic priors of generative AI with the geometric stability of rendering engines.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)

We aim to build a two-stage pipeline: **Generative Expansion** followed by **Geometric Distillation**.

### 1. Morphable Multi-View Diffusion Model (MMDM)
We will design a diffusion-based generator capable of synthesizing novel views of a subject.
*   **Conditioning Strategy:** To ensure the generated images adhere to specific 3D geometries and expressions, we will condition the network on "attribute maps" rendered from a parametric face model (3DMM). These maps will explicitly encode head pose, expression-induced deformations, and camera ray directions.
*   **Architecture:** We will adapt a pre-trained latent diffusion model, modifying the attention mechanisms to support cross-view communication (3D attention), allowing the model to reason about the subject's appearance across different viewpoints simultaneously.

### 2. Stochastic Input/Output (I/O) Conditioning
A key technical challenge is that diffusion models typically have a fixed, small context window (e.g., creating 4 images at a time), which is insufficient for generating a full dataset.
*   **The Scaling Mechanism:** To overcome this, we propose a stochastic sampling procedure during the inference phase. Inside the iterative denoising loop, we will dynamically shuffle inputs. At each step, the model will see a random subset of the original reference images and a random subset of the noisy "target" images being generated.
*   **Logic:** This ensures that information propagates globally across the entire set of desired outputs. Even if we generate hundreds of frames, every frame will eventually be conditioned on every reference image, ensuring global identity and lighting consistency without exploding memory requirements.

### 3. Real-Time 4D Reconstruction
Once the MMDM has generated a comprehensive set of views and expressions, we will use this synthetic dataset to optimize an animatable representation.
*   **Hybrid Representation:** We will utilize 3D Gaussian Splatting anchored to a deformable mesh surface. By attaching Gaussian primitives to the triangles of a tracked face mesh, we gain the animation control of a rig while retaining the volumetric rendering quality of splats.
*   **Detail Refinement:** To capture fine-grained details (like wrinkles) that the coarse mesh cannot represent, we will employ a lightweight neural network to predict texture/deformation offsets in UV space based on the current expression parameters.

## Expected Contribution
*   **Scalability:** A unified method that creates photorealistic avatars regardless of whether the input is a single image or a video sequence, with quality improving as data increases.
*   **Generative Consistency:** A novel stochastic conditioning algorithm that allows multi-view diffusion models to scale to an arbitrary number of consistent views, solving the "context window" limitation of current generative architectures.
*   **Real-Time Usability:** By distilling heavy diffusion priors into a Gaussian Splatting representation, we enable real-time rendering and animation, making the high-quality avatars practical for interactive applications.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

*   **Training Datasets:** 
    *   A collection of monocular and multi-view videos comprising VFHQ, MEAD, Ava-256, and Nersemble.
    *   Total volume: 24.6k video sequences, 41.3M frames, spanning 6317 diverse subjects.
*   **Evaluation Datasets:**
    *   **Self-reenactment:** 9 multi-view capture sequences from the Nersemble dataset. 4 of 16 camera viewpoints were held out for evaluation (100 frames each). Reference images were selected from the remaining viewpoints (1, 10, or 100 images). Azimuth/elevation range: $\pm 55^{\circ}$ and $\pm 20^{\circ}$.
    *   **Cross-reenactment:** 10 reference images from the FFHQ dataset. Driving videos included 5 from VFHQ (normal expression range) and 5 from Nersemble (extreme expressions).
*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **Photometric Accuracy:** Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS).
    *   **Identity Preservation:** Cosine Similarity of Identity Embeddings (CSIM).
    *   **Temporal Consistency:** Just Objectionable Difference (JOD).
    *   **Human Preference:** Visual Quality (VQ), Expression Transfer (ET), 3D Structure (3DS), Temporal Consistency (TC), Overall Preference.
*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   **Single-view reconstruction:** GAGAvatar, Portrait4D-v2, Real3D-Portrait, Voodoo3D.
    *   **Multi-view reconstruction:** DiffusionRig, FlashAvatar, GaussianAvatars.
    *   **Internal Ablations:** "no MMDM" (reconstructing directly from reference images without generation), "MMDM only" (direct prediction of target frames without 4D avatar reconstruction), "w/o expr" (no expression maps), "w/o ray" (no view ray conditioning), "w/o stochastic" (no stochastic I/O sampling), "w/o U-Net" (no deformation U-Net), "w/o LPIPS" (no LPIPS loss).
*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Training Hardware:** 8 $\times$ H100 GPUs.
    *   **Training Time:** Approx. 2 weeks.
    *   **Optimization:** AdamW optimizer, learning rate $10^{-4}$, batch size 64.
    *   **Training Schedule:** 100k total iterations (80k with 1 reference frame, 20k with $\le 4$ randomly chosen reference frames). Dropout on conditioning signals (prob 0.1). Classifier-free guidance used during inference.
    *   **Generation (Inference):** Generated $G=840$ images ($512 \times 512$ resolution) using 250 DDIM steps with stochastic I/O conditioning. Time: ~4 hours on 4 $\times$ RTX 6000 GPUs.
    *   **4D Reconstruction:** 100k iterations (~4 hours on 1 RTX 6000 GPU).
    *   **Rendering Resolution:** $768 \times 768$ (cross-reenactment, 33 fps), $1100 \times 1604$ (self-reenactment, 16 fps).

## 3. Qualitative Observations

*   **Generative Fidelity (Single Image):** We observed that the method reconstructs 4D avatars from a single reference image with higher visual fidelity than previous generative baselines.
*   **Generative Fidelity (Multiple Images):** We observed that visual quality improves with the number of reference images (e.g., from 1 to 10 to 100), specifically in identity preservation (CSIM) and sharpness.
*   **Comparison to Baselines (Self-Reenactment):**
    *   FlashAvatar produced results with competitive PSNR but noticeably blurrier output images compared to our method, resulting in lower LPIPS scores.
    *   GaussianAvatars, FlashAvatar, and the "no-MMDM" ablation tended to overfit to the reference viewpoints and failed to generalize well to novel views.
    *   The "MMDM only" ablation (predicting frames directly) achieved the highest photometric quality (PSNR) but suffered from reduced temporal consistency (lower JOD) compared to the full 4D avatar reconstruction.
*   **Comparison to Baselines (Cross-Reenactment):**
    *   Our method faithfully captured driving expressions while maintaining the likeness of the reference subject, even under challenging view directions.
    *   We observed that our method generated plausible results in occluded regions (e.g., earrings, shawls) that were visible in the reference but occluded in the driving video.
    *   High-frequency details (e.g., freckles) were better recovered compared to baselines.
    *   While Real3D achieved slightly higher CSIM scores, human evaluators overwhelmingly preferred our method (96% preference) over Real3D across all quality criteria.
*   **Ablation Observations:**
    *   Removing expression deformation maps ("w/o expr") significantly impacted photometric quality.
    *   Removing view direction conditioning ("w/o ray") had a less significant impact than removing expression maps.
    *   Stochastic I/O sampling improved PSNR, CSIM, and JOD compared to non-stochastic sampling ("w/o stochastic").
    *   Removing the U-Net for expression-dependent deformations reduced the capability to model fine details like wrinkles, lowering PSNR and LPIPS.
    *   Removing the LPIPS loss improved PSNR numerically but degraded perceptual quality (LPIPS).
*   **Extensions and Editing:**
    *   We successfully demonstrated 4D appearance editing (virtual make-up) and relighting by applying the method to reference images edited with off-the-shelf 2D models.
    *   We successfully drove the avatars using audio input via a speech-to-3DMM prediction method.
    *   We generated $360^{\circ}$ views, though we observed generation quality limitations at the back of the head due to a lack of training data for that specific angle.

  - Filename: figure_2.png
  - Caption: Figure 2. Overview of CAP4D. (a) The method takes as input an arbitrary number of reference images Iref that are encoded into the latent space of a variational autoencoder [74]. An off-the-shelf face tracker estimates a 3DMM, Mref, for each reference image, from which we derive conditioning signals that describe camera view direction, Vref, head pose Pref, and expression Eref. We associate additional conditioning signals with each input noisy latent image based on the desired generated viewpoints, poses, and expressions (see Fig. 3). The MMDM generates images through a stochastic input–output conditioning procedure that randomly samples reference images and generated images during each step of the iterative image generation process. (b) The generated and reference images are used with the tracked and sampled 3DMMs to reconstruct a 4D avatar based on a 3D Gaussian splatting representation [47, 71].
--------------------------------------------------
Item 2:
  - Filename: figure_3.png
  - Caption: Figure 3. MMDM conditioning. We preprocess each reference image based on the estimated 3DMM model. We obtain a tightfitting bounding box around the head region (a), which is squared and enlarged (b). We crop the image to the square bounding box and remove the background. Then, we update camera intrinsics to the updated crop and obtain the conditioning images Vref (ray directions), Pref (3D pose map), Eref (expression deformation map), and the reference and outcropping masks. We follow the same process for generated images.
--------------------------------------------------
Item 3:
  - Filename: figure_6.png
  - Caption: Figure 6. Extensions. We demonstrate 4D appearance editing and relighting by applying CAP4D to images edited using off-the-shelf models [68, 111]. We also animate CAP4D avatars with a method that predicts 3DMM expressions from speech [96] (see supp. videos).
--------------------------------------------------
Item 4:

  - Caption: Figure 7. MMDM-generated 360◦ views.
--------------------------------------------------
Item 5:
  - Filename: figure_4.png
  - Caption: Figure 4. Self-reenactment. Our approach is more realistic than baseline methods for self-reenactment from a single reference image (row 1), 10 reference images (row 2), and 100 reference images (row 3). The MMDM output (MMDM only) produces the most realistic output at the cost of temporal consistency compared to our reconstructed 4D Avatar (CAP4D).
--------------------------------------------------
Item 6:
  - Filename: figure_5.png
  - Caption: Figure 5. Cross-reenactment. Avatars are reconstructed from a single reference image (col. 1), and their expressions are driven by frames of a driving video (col. 2). The camera moves according to the indicated horizontal (H) and vertical (V) view angles. CAP4D faithfully recovers the driving expression and maintains the likeness of the reference subject from challenging view directions. It generates plausible results in occluded regions based on the reference image (e.g., earrings, row 1) and recovers high-frequency details (freckles, row 1).
--------------------------------------------------
Item 7:
  - Filename: figure_1.png
  - Caption: Figure 1. We present CAP4D: a method that generates 4D portrait avatars based on an arbitrary number of reference images and animates them in real time. Our approach uses a morphable multi-view diffusion model to predict novel views with unseen expressions. For each subject, we generate hundreds of such views and train an animatable avatar using a representation based on 3D Gaussian splatting. Our method demonstrates state-of-the-art results for portrait view synthesis from a single image, monocular videos, or multi-view camera setups based on visual quality, identity consistency, 3D structure, and temporal consistency.
--------------------------------------------------

Figures are located in the figures/ directory and should be referenced appropriately in the paper using standard \includegraphics commands.

prompt.text:
Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# CVPR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the latex paper writing process for CVPR 2025.

## Language
All manuscripts must be in English.

## Submission Policies & Anonymity
CVPR reviewing is double-blind. Authors must not know the names of the reviewers, and reviewers must not know the names of the authors.

* **No Identifying Information:** Do not provide information that may identify the authors in the acknowledgments (e.g., co-workers and grant IDs) or in the supplementary material.
* **Links:** Do not provide links to websites that identify the authors.
* **GitHub:** Links to GitHub must be anonymous.
* **Self-Citation:** If you need to cite any of your own papers that are being submitted concurrently, include anonymized versions in the supplementary material and cite them as anonymous. Do not use the words "my" or "our" when citing previous work; treat your own prior work as if it were written by someone else (e.g., "Smith et al. showed..." rather than "We showed...").

## Paper length
Papers, excluding the references section, must be no longer than eight pages in length.
The references section will not be included in the page count, and there is no limit on the length of the references section.
For example, a paper of eight pages with two pages of references would have a total length of 10 pages.

Overlength papers, or papers where margins and formatting are deemed significantly altered, will simply not be reviewed.

## Mathematics
Please number all of your sections and displayed equations as in these examples:
```latex
\begin{equation}
  E = m\cdot c^2
  \label{eq:important}
\end{equation}
```
and
```latex
\begin{equation}
  v = a\cdot t.
  \label{eq:also-important}
\end{equation}
```

## Formatting your paper
All text must be in a two-column format.
The total allowable size of the text area is $6\frac78$ inches (17.46 cm) wide by $8\frac78$ inches (22.54 cm) high.
Columns are to be $3\frac14$ inches (8.25 cm) wide, with a $\frac{5}{16}$ inch (0.8 cm) space between them.
The main title (on the first page) should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge of the page.
The second and following pages should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge.
On all pages, the bottom margin should be $1\frac{1}{8}$ inches (2.86 cm) from the bottom edge of the page for $8.5 \times 11$-inch paper;
for A4 paper, approximately $1\frac{5}{8}$ inches (4.13 cm) from the bottom edge of the page.

### Type style and fonts
Wherever Times is specified, Times Roman may also be used. If neither is available on your word processor, please use the font closest in appearance to Times to which you have access.

### Main Title
Center the title $1\frac{3}{8}$ inches (3.49 cm) from the top edge of the first page. The title should be in Times 14-point, boldface type. Capitalize the first letter of nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs; do not capitalize articles, coordinate conjunctions, or prepositions (unless the title begins with such a word).

The ABSTRACT and MAIN TEXT are to be in a two-column format.

### Main Text
Type main text in 10-point Times, single-spaced.
Do NOT use double-spacing.
All paragraphs should be indented 1 pica (approx.~$\frac{1}{6}$ inch or 0.422 cm). Make sure your text is fully justified---that is, flush left and flush right. Please do not place any additional blank lines between paragraphs.

Figure and table captions should be 9-point Roman type as in \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short}. 
Short captions should be centred.

\noindent Callouts should be 9-point Helvetica, non-boldface type. Initially capitalize only the first word of section titles and first-, second-, and third-order headings.

#### First-order Headings
For example, {\large \bf 1. Introduction} should be Times 12-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one blank line after.

#### Second-order Headings
For example, { \bf 1.1. Database elements} should be Times 11-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one after.
If you require a third-order heading (we discourage it), use 10-point Times, boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, preceded by one blank line, followed by a period and your text on the same line.

### Footnotes
Please use \footnote{This is what a footnote looks like.
It often distracts the reader from the main flow of the argument.} sparingly.

Indeed, try to avoid footnotes altogether and include necessary peripheral observations in the text (within parentheses, if you prefer, as in this sentence). If you wish to use a footnote, place it at the bottom of the column on the page on which it is referenced.
Use Times 8-point type, single-spaced.

### Cross-references
For the benefit of author(s) and readers, please use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
```
command for cross-referencing to figures, tables, equations, or sections.

This will automatically insert the appropriate label alongside the cross-reference as in this example:
```latex
\begin{quotation}
  To see how our method outperforms previous work, please see \cref{fig:onecol} and \cref{tab:example}.
  It is also possible to refer to multiple targets as once, \eg~to \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short-a}.
  You may also return to \cref{sec:formatting} or look at \cref{eq:also-important}.
\end{quotation}
```
If you do not wish to abbreviate the label, for example at the beginning of the sentence, you can use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \Cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
command. Here is an example:
\begin{quotation}
  \Cref{fig:onecol} is also quite important.
\end{quotation}
```

## Illustrations, graphs, and photographs
All graphics should be centered.
In \LaTeX, avoid using the \texttt{center} environment for this purpose, as this adds potentially unwanted whitespace.
Instead use
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \centering
\end{verbatim}}
```
at the beginning of your figure.

Please ensure that any point you wish to make is resolvable in a printed copy of the paper. Resize fonts in figures to match the font in the body text, and choose line widths that render effectively in print.

When placing figures in \LaTeX, it's almost always best to use \verb+\includegraphics+, and to specify the figure width as a multiple of the line width as in the example below

references.text:
## Problem Statement
The creation of photorealistic, animatable 4D portrait avatars currently faces a stark dichotomy in capture requirements. High-fidelity methods, such as those relying on multi-view stereo or neural rendering, depend on elaborate studio setups with camera arrays capturing hundreds of reference images. Conversely, recent generative methods can produce avatars from a single "in-the-wild" image but suffer from poor 3D consistency and reduced visual fidelity compared to multi-view techniques.

There is currently no unified framework capable of scaling seamlessly between these two extremes. Specifically, we lack a robust methodology to reconstruct photorealistic 4D avatars from an arbitrary number of inputs—ranging from a single snapshot to hundreds of frames—that can still be rendered and animated in real-time. Existing diffusion-based solutions are largely limited to static 2D outputs or computationally expensive inference that prohibits real-time interaction.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose **CAP4D**, a two-stage framework that decouples view synthesis from real-time rendering. Our core hypothesis is that we can bridge the gap between single-image and multi-view reconstruction by training a **Morphable Multi-View Diffusion Model (MMDM)**. This model will leverage a stochastic conditioning mechanism to "hallucinate" a dense, multi-view dataset from sparse inputs (down to a single image) by adhering to strict 3D Morphable Model (3DMM) constraints.

By generating a comprehensive set of synthetic views with varied poses and expressions, we can subsequently distill this information into an animatable **3D Gaussian Splatting** representation. This approach combines the generative prior of large-scale diffusion models with the real-time rendering efficiency of Gaussian Splats.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

Our approach consists of two distinct stages: (1) Generative Multi-View Synthesis via MMDM, and (2) 4D Avatar Reconstruction via Gaussian Splatting.

### 1. Morphable Multi-View Diffusion Model (MMDM)

We will develop an MMDM that learns the joint probability of a set of generated images $\mathbf{I}_{gen}$ given a set of reference images $\mathbf{I}_{ref}$ and their respective conditioning signals $\mathbf{C}$:
$$ P(\mathbf{I}_{gen} | \mathbf{I}_{ref}, \mathbf{C}_{ref}, \mathbf{C}_{gen}) $$

**Architecture:**
The model will be initialized from Stable Diffusion 2.1. We will modify the U-Net architecture by replacing the 2D attention layers following 2D residual blocks with **3D attention layers**. These layers will attend across two spatial dimensions and one dimension representing the image batch (input images), allowing information sharing between processed latents. We will remove text-conditioning cross-attention layers.

**Conditioning Signals:**
To enforce precise control over pose and expression, we will condition the diffusion model on rasterized maps derived from a tracked 3DMM (FLAME). For each reference image $r$ and target generated image $g$, we define the conditioning signal $\mathbf{C} = \{ \mathbf{P}, \mathbf{E}, \mathbf{V}, \mathbf{B} \}$, concatenated to the latent inputs:

1.  **3D Pose Maps ($\mathbf{P}$):** We will associate each vertex of the mesh $\mathbf{M}$ with its canonical 3D position in a template mesh $\mathbf{T}$. We rasterize these attributes to form the map:
    $$ \mathbf{p}^{(r)}_{ref} = \gamma \left[ \mathrm{RASTERIZE} \left( \mathbf{m}_{ref}^{(r)}, \mathbf{T}, \mathbf{\Pi}_{ref}^{(r)} \right) \right] $$
    Here, $\gamma$ is a positional encoding function (sine/cosine mapping), $\mathbf{\Pi}$ is the camera projection matrix, and $\mathrm{RASTERIZE}$ renders the template coordinates from the specific camera view.

2.  **Expression Deformation Maps ($\mathbf{E}$):** To capture subtle expression changes, we calculate the 3D offset of each vertex relative to a neutral expression mesh (sharing the same shape parameters). We rasterize these offsets (without positional encoding) to create $\mathbf{E}$.

3.  **View Direction Maps ($\mathbf{V}$) and Masks ($\mathbf{B}$):** $\mathbf{V}$ encodes per-pixel ray directions relative to the first view's reference frame. $\mathbf{B}$ is a binary mask indicating if an input is a reference or generated image.

**Stochastic Input/Output (I/O) Conditioning:**
Standard multi-view diffusion is limited by GPU memory (typically handling $\approx 4$ views). To scale to arbitrary inputs and output hundreds of views, we will implement a stochastic I/O procedure during the reverse diffusion process.

Let $R$ be the total available reference images and $G$ be the total desired generated images. In each diffusion timestep $t$:
1.  We verify the set of generated latents $\mathbf{Z}_{gen, t}$.
2.  We enter an inner loop to process the generated images in batches of size $G'$.
3.  For each batch, we randomly sample (without replacement) a subset of $R'$ reference images from the total set $R$.
4.  The model predicts the noise $\epsilon$ using this random subset of references and the current batch of generated latents.
5.  We apply the denoising step (DDIM) to update $\mathbf{Z}_{gen}$.

This ensures that over the full diffusion trajectory, the generated images are conditioned on the entire set of available reference images, maintaining global consistency.

### 2. Robust 4D Avatar Reconstruction

The second stage converts the generated multi-view imagery into a real-time 4D representation.

**Representation:**
We will utilize **3D Gaussian Splatting**, where Gaussians are attached to the triangles of a FLAME head mesh.
*   We will remesh the FLAME topology to ensure pixel-aligned vertices in a UV space of resolution $128 \times 128$.
*   This creates a 1-to-1 mapping between surface geometry and texture space.

**Dynamics Modeling:**
To model fine-grained, expression-dependent deformations (e.g., wrinkles) that the coarse FLAME mesh cannot capture, we will introduce a **deformation U-Net**.
*   Input: Offsets in UV space derived from the expression blendshapes.
*   Output: A UV deformation map predicting fine-grained displacements.
*   The system uses a modified FLAME mesh with separate upper and lower jaw structures to better handle mouth dynamics.

**Optimization:**
We will optimize the opacity, covariance, and color of the Gaussians, along with the deformation U-Net weights, using the synthesized dataset $\mathbf{I}_{gen}$ and the original $\mathbf{I}_{ref}$. The loss function will include:
1.  Photometric reconstruction loss against the generated/reference images.
2.  **Laplacian regularization** on the predicted deformation map.
3.  **$L_2$ regularization** on the relative deformation and rotation of every Gaussian splat.
4.  **LPIPS loss** ($\lambda_{LPIPS}$) to ensure perceptual quality, increasing linearly with iterations.

## Expected Contribution
We anticipate that CAP4D will provide the following theoretical and practical contributions:
1.  **Unified Scalability:** A single architecture capable of handling the full spectrum of input constraints, from one-shot generation to dense multi-view reconstruction.
2.  **Stochastic Diffusion Consistency:** A novel conditioning algorithm that allows diffusion models to utilize arbitrary numbers of reference images beyond the training batch size limits, ensuring identity consistency across hundreds of generated views.
3.  **Real-Time Fidelity:** The successful distillation of generative diffusion priors into a 3D Gaussian representation will enable real-time rendering (30+ fps) of photorealistic avatars with dynamic expressions, bridging the gap between offline generative quality and interactive graphics applications.

preinstalled.en: orchestrator image: upstream code at the pin (unmodified), uv-locked dependencies, the docker CLI (a shim adds proxy and CA to sibling containers); agent image: upstream's own agent-cli Dockerfile

notes.benchmark_paths: A benchmark item's paths are mounted into the agent containers unless upstream mounts the same path itself (/workspace and below, /home/agent-home, /task-source, /run, /tmp): those are left out and listed in logs/sibling-mounts.txt. The agents work in upstream's own /workspace (the run directory), so a deliverable the official prompt names under such a path is not written where the run collects it.
notes.venue: paper.paper_format=iclr for every task. The system has only iclr and alife specs and does not choose a venue itself; ICML and NeurIPS templates and a system-chosen venue are unsupported.
notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. The paradigm is optimisation of a scalar score: the task-drafting phase (documented as experimental) turns the brief into an evaluator and a seed program.
notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.
notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.
notes.search: Provider server-side web search is switched off in every sibling by the agent CLIs' own system settings, bind-mounted read-only by the docker shim: Claude Code /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (permissions.deny WebSearch), Codex /etc/codex/config.toml (web_search="disabled") and /etc/codex/requirements.toml (allowed_web_search_modes=["disabled"]). Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
notes.key_exposure: The provider key is in the environment of the agent containers (upstream env-file mechanism) and therefore visible to commands the agent runs. Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 was tried and aborts: it needs bubblewrap, which the unmodified upstream agent image lacks.
notes.gpu: gpus=1 is wired (container.gpu_count, harness GPU evaluation) but was not exercised.
notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

network.search: Provider server-side web search is switched off in every sibling by the agent CLIs' own system settings, bind-mounted read-only by the docker shim: Claude Code /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (permissions.deny WebSearch), Codex /etc/codex/config.toml (web_search="disabled") and /etc/codex/requirements.toml (allowed_web_search_modes=["disabled"]). Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
network.web_access: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.

tools.permissions: upstream's own agent settings; provider web search denied by managed settings (Claude Code permissions.deny WebSearch, Codex web_search="disabled")

preinstalled.zh: 编排镜像：上游代码（固定提交、未改）、uv 锁定依赖、docker CLI（经 shim 给兄弟容器加代理和 CA）；agent 镜像：上游自己的 agent-cli Dockerfile
preinstalled.en: orchestrator image: upstream code at the pin (unmodified), uv-locked dependencies, the docker CLI (a shim adds proxy and CA to sibling containers); agent image: upstream's own agent-cli Dockerfile

notes.benchmark_paths: A benchmark item's paths are mounted into the agent containers unless upstream mounts the same path itself (/workspace and below, /home/agent-home, /task-source, /run, /tmp): those are left out and listed in logs/sibling-mounts.txt. The agents work in upstream's own /workspace (the run directory), so a deliverable the official prompt names under such a path is not written where the run collects it.
notes.venue: paper.paper_format=iclr for every task. The system has only iclr and alife specs and does not choose a venue itself; ICML and NeurIPS templates and a system-chosen venue are unsupported.
notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. The paradigm is optimisation of a scalar score: the task-drafting phase (documented as experimental) turns the brief into an evaluator and a seed program.
notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.
notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.
notes.search: Provider server-side web search is switched off in every sibling by the agent CLIs' own system settings, bind-mounted read-only by the docker shim: Claude Code /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (permissions.deny WebSearch), Codex /etc/codex/config.toml (web_search="disabled") and /etc/codex/requirements.toml (allowed_web_search_modes=["disabled"]). Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
notes.key_exposure: The provider key is in the environment of the agent containers (upstream env-file mechanism) and therefore visible to commands the agent runs. Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 was tried and aborts: it needs bubblewrap, which the unmodified upstream agent image lacks.
notes.gpu: gpus=1 is wired (container.gpu_count, harness GPU evaluation) but was not exercised.
notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

agent.name: none
agent.how: no coding agent: a 23-stage prompt-chain pipeline over the Anthropic Messages API

network.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).

tools.permissions: no tool calls (requests carry model, messages, max_tokens); generated experiments run as plain subprocesses in the container

preinstalled.zh: python:3.11 bookworm；上游代码按 PYTHONPATH 使用；pdflatex + bibtex；CPU 版 PyTorch 和 numpy、scipy、scikit-learn、pandas、matplotlib 等（constraints.txt 固定）
preinstalled.en: python:3.11 bookworm; upstream code via PYTHONPATH; pdflatex + bibtex; CPU PyTorch with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib and more (pinned by constraints.txt)

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

agent.name: none
agent.how: no external coding agent: EvoScientist's in-process sub-agents (LangChain deepagents)

tools.permissions: think_tool, deepagents built-ins, EvoSkills skills and an execute shell; skill_manager not registered; no search tool

preinstalled.zh: 上游锁定依赖（uv sync --frozen）加兼容补丁 compat.patch；TeX Live（含 fonts-extra、latexmk）；给 agent 用的研究 Python 环境 /opt/research
preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
